academicContentSignals: Resume definition: short, highly structured summary of education, work history, and life experiences to secure a job interview.
Resume 4-section architecture: fixed first section (professional metadata), two adjustable middle sections (education, experience), fixed final section (honors and activities).
Metadata formatting: 16-18pt bold name, non-QQ email, phone, location, portfolio links for art/design.
Education section: reverse chronological order, GPA only if 3.0/70% or higher, limit to middle school and above.
Experience section: action statement formula: [action verb] + [task description] + [execution method] + [quantifiable, verifiable result]; avoid 'duties included' or 'responsible for'.
Honors and activities: include role title, organization, dates; eligible entries include student council, sports captain, clubs, volunteer hours.
Resume styles: chronological, extracurricular, clinical, co-op/academic, customer service.
No paid work experience strategies: count school fundraisers, academic projects, gig work, volunteer hours; add job-specific objective.
Final audit rules: 1-2 pages, no personal pronouns, no AI generation, peer review.
Plagiarism rule: any use of translation tools or AI results in automatic zero.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects incorrect option on diagnostic question diag-olc4o-q1
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students believe a resume should be a detailed account of their entire life and work history, rather than a concise summary designed to secure a job interview.

miniLesson.explain: A resume is a short, highly structured summary of education, work history, and relevant life experiences, with the sole purpose of securing a job interview. It is not an autobiography or a job application form. The goal is to get an interview, not to get hired directly.
miniLesson.example: Consider two resume summaries: (1) 'I was born in 2000, attended Springfield Elementary, and have always enjoyed reading. I worked at a grocery store for two years where I stocked shelves and helped customers.' (2) 'Detail-oriented high school graduate with 2 years of customer service experience at a busy grocery store, recognized for efficiency and positive customer feedback.' The second summary is targeted and designed to get an interview; the first is too detailed and unfocused.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of your resume as a movie trailer – it highlights the best parts to make the employer want to see the full movie (the interview).

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a resume? Choose the best answer: (A) To provide a detailed account of your entire life and work history. (B) To secure a job interview. (C) To apply directly for a job and be hired immediately. (D) To showcase all your skills without focusing on a specific job.

Read the following resume excerpt: 'I was head of the student council for two years, during which I organized events and represented the student body. I also volunteered at a local shelter and played soccer.' Is this excerpt focused on getting an interview? Why or why not? (Hint: Consider if it is too detailed or lacks a targeted purpose.)
guidedPractice.answer: No, this excerpt is too detailed and reads like a biography. It includes unnecessary personal details and does not directly market the candidate's skills to get an interview. A better summary would highlight quantifiable achievements and target the job.

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite the following resume summary to focus on getting an interview. Original: 'I am a hardworking student who has taken many courses and participated in several clubs. I have good grades and I am responsible.' Ensure the new version is concise and emphasizes interview-worthy points.
guidedPractice.answer: Revised: 'Honour-roll student with strong organizational and leadership skills gained through active participation in three school clubs. Consistently meets deadlines and excels in collaborative projects, aiming to contribute to a dynamic team environment.'

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly identified a resume bullet point that lacks quantifiable results.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think listing duties without quantifiable results is sufficient for a resume.

miniLesson.explain: Every experience bullet point on a resume must follow the action statement formula: [action verb] + [task description] + [execution method] + [quantifiable, verifiable result]. Employers want to see the impact of your work, not just a list of duties. Numbers make your achievements concrete and memorable.
miniLesson.example: coordinated school fundraising events, leading a team of 10 volunteers, raising $2,000 for local charities.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: If there's no number, your resume won't stand out.

guidedPractice.prompt: Does the following bullet point include a quantifiable result? 'Supervised a team during the event.'
guidedPractice.answer: No, it lacks a number or measurable outcome.

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite the following vague bullet to include a quantifiable result: 'Helped organize a fundraiser.'
guidedPractice.answer: Coordinated a school fundraiser, leading a team of 10 volunteers and raising $2,000 for local charities.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write a bullet point for a volunteer experience at a community clean-up. Use quantifiable results.
guidedPractice.answer: Led a team of 10 volunteers to clean up Riverside Park, collecting 200 pounds of trash and planting 50 trees.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selected wrong option on diag-olc4o-q3, believing AI/translation tool use is acceptable.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: You think that using AI or translation software to generate part or all of your resume is okay, perhaps because you believe you can edit it or that resumes are not academic work. However, the course policy clearly states that any work generated by AI or translation tools will receive an automatic zero, with no exceptions.

miniLesson.explain: The course has a strict plagiarism policy: any work fully or partially generated via translation tools or AI receives an automatic zero score. This applies to the resume assignment. Using AI or translation software is considered cheating because it prevents you from developing your own writing skills. Even if you edit the AI output, it is still not your original work. You must write everything yourself and have a peer review your draft. The purpose of the assignment is to practice real-world resume writing, and using AI undermines that learning.
miniLesson.example: If you use an AI tool to write a bullet point like 'Managed a team of 5 volunteers, increasing event attendance by 20%,' and then submit it as your own, that is plagiarism. You would receive a zero on the assignment, and it could affect your course grade. Instead, you should write your own bullet points based on your actual experiences, using the action statement formula taught in class.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: AI = zero. Never use AI or translation tools for any part of your resume. Write it yourself, then get a peer to review.

guidedPractice.prompt: True or False: It is acceptable to use an AI tool to help you generate ideas for your resume, as long as you rewrite the ideas in your own words.
guidedPractice.answer: False. According to the course policy, any work generated by AI, even partially, receives a zero. You must not use AI at all, even for ideas.

guidedPractice.prompt: Choose the correct statement: A) If I edit AI-generated content, it becomes my own work. B) The resume is not an academic paper, so using AI is allowed. C) Using AI or translation tools for any part of the resume results in an automatic zero.
Explain in 2-3 sentences why the course policy prohibits AI and translation tools for the resume assignment, and describe one alternative strategy to get help without using AI.
guidedPractice.answer: The course policy prohibits AI and translation tools because the resume assignment is designed to develop your own writing skills and produce authentic work. Using AI bypasses the learning process and is considered academic dishonesty. Instead, you can ask a peer or teacher for feedback on your draft, or use the action verb lists and examples provided in the lesson.

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly includes personal pronouns (I, me, my) in resume bullet points.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think it is acceptable to use first-person pronouns in resumes, not understanding that professional resumes should avoid them to maintain conciseness and formality.

miniLesson.explain: Resumes must avoid personal pronouns like 'I', 'me', 'my', or 'we' because the reader knows the resume is about you. Using pronouns makes the writing less concise and less professional. Instead, start each bullet with a strong action verb and focus on the task and result.
miniLesson.example:
Incorrect: 'I coordinated a team of volunteers for the school carnival.'
Correct: 'Coordinated a team of 10 volunteers for the school carnival, increasing attendance by 25%.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of a resume as a list of your achievements—no 'I' needed; let your actions speak.

guidedPractice.prompt:
Which of the following bullet points is written correctly for a resume?
A. I organized a bake sale that raised $500.
B. Organized a bake sale that raised $500.
C. My organization of a bake sale raised $500.
guidedPractice.answer: B. Organized a bake sale that raised $500.

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite the following bullet point to remove personal pronouns and add a quantifiable result: 'I was responsible for managing the school's recycling program.'
guidedPractice.answer: Managed the school's recycling program, coordinating 5 student volunteers and reducing waste by 20%.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write a complete resume bullet point for this scenario: You led a team in a school fundraiser. Include action verb, task, method, and quantifiable result, without using any personal pronouns.
guidedPractice.answer: Led a team of 8 students in a car wash fundraiser, raising $1,200 for the school band.

cards.question: What is the primary purpose of a resume?
options: To provide a detailed account of your entire life and work history.
To secure a job interview.
To apply directly for a job and be hired on the spot.
To showcase all your skills without focusing on a specific job.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands the resume's primary goal.
misconceptions: A resume is a short, targeted summary, not a full biography.
✓ Correct! The sole purpose of a resume is to get you an interview.
The resume itself doesn't get you hired; it gets you an interview.
A resume should be tailored to the job and focused on landing an interview.
cards.successCriteria: Student selects the correct purpose: securing a job interview.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of the importance of communication skills in their everyday lives - at school, at work, and at home.
cards.alignmentNote: Question directly assesses understanding of resume's real-world communication purpose.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think the resume is a detailed autobiography or job application form rather than a tool to get an interview.

cards.question: Which of the following experience bullet points best follows the action statement formula?
options: Responsible for organizing the school fundraiser.
Organized a school food drive, managing 15 volunteers and collecting 500 items for the local food bank.
Helped with several school events throughout the year.
Duties included coordinating volunteers and managing logistics.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can identify a correctly written experience bullet with quantification.
misconceptions: This uses 'responsible for' and lacks a quantifiable result.
✓ Correct! It has an action verb, task, method, and quantifiable result (15 volunteers, 500 items).
Too vague; no specific task, method, or quantifiable result.
Uses 'duties included' and lacks quantifiable results.
cards.successCriteria: Student selects the option that includes action verb, task, method, and quantifiable result.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: Question tests application of action statement formula with quantifiable results.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think listing duties without results is sufficient.

cards.question: According to the course policy, what happens if a student uses AI or translation software to generate their resume?
options: It is acceptable as long as the student edits the AI-generated content.
The resume will be rejected and the student will receive a zero score.
The teacher will deduct a few marks but the work will still be accepted.
It is allowed because resumes are not considered academic work.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows the course rule against AI/translation tool use.
misconceptions: The course policy states that any AI or translation tool use results in a zero, even with editing.
✓ Correct! Full or partial AI generation is not allowed and results in a zero.
The policy is stricter: automatic zero, not a partial deduction.
The rule applies to all written work, including resumes.
cards.successCriteria: Student selects that the resume will be rejected and the student will receive a zero.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate understanding of their own roles and responsibilities in the learning process.
cards.alignmentNote: Question addresses plagiarism rule; best available node is resume-purpose, but expectation C2 for responsibility is more apt.
cards.commonMisconception: Students believe using AI is acceptable if they edit the output.

cards.question: Which of the following is an appropriate bullet point to include in a resume?
options: I coordinated a team of volunteers for the school carnival.
Coordinated a team of 10 volunteers for the school carnival, increasing attendance by 25%.
My responsibilities included coordinating volunteers and managing schedules.
We worked together to make the carnival a success.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows to avoid first-person pronouns in resume writing.
misconceptions: Avoid first-person pronouns ('I') in resume bullet points.
✓ Correct! No personal pronouns, action verb, and quantifiable result.
Uses 'my' and 'included', which are not recommended in resume writing.
cards.successCriteria: Student selects the option that avoids personal pronouns and uses strong action verbs.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.
cards.alignmentNote: Question checks understanding of resume formatting convention regarding pronoun use.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may use 'I' or 'my' because they think it sounds natural.
